While you can't do this, banks often do this. This was the 2008 financial crisis in a nutshell. For example, AIG would take a bunch of crappy mortgages, package them into a MBS, and sell them to BoA. BoA would package these MBSes into a CDO, then sell them back to other buyers (likely including AIG). Then AIG would turn their CDOs into synthetic CDOs or CDSes and sell them back to BoA. It was a cycle of borrowed money. The ultimate circlejerk.

Selling debt is perfectly normal and reasonable. The problems happen when the buyer doesn't do their due diligence and buys bad debts with no collateral.

In the case of the subprime crisis, the government was guaranteeing everyone's mortgages to "stabilise the market." This created a false sense of security and by the 90s/2000s, banks were handing out mortgages like candy.

This is a kind of limited/simplified view of the subprime crisis that doesn't taker into account the main engine for it. You're right that the issue was mortgages were being handed out "like candy" because the lenders didn't care about the creditworthiness of the buyer, but the reason behind this wasn't the government guaranteeing mortgages (I don't know what you mean by that -- the government never 100% backed anyone's mortgage).

Basically, a MBS (mortgage backed security) consists of a lot of mortgages bundled together and organized in tranches. The highest (AAA) tranche consists of loans to people with 700+ credit ratings, while the lowest tranche (C) consists of people with like 450 (ie quite likely to default on their loans). The lower tranche pays much better interest because it's a higher risk. So far, so good.

What happened was that banks took a lot of the B and C tranches -- the crappy loans -- and bundled those into a CDO (collateralized debt obligation) . Their reasoning was that not everyone would go bankrupt at once. They took these bundles of B and C tranches and sent the off to Moody's, which rated them AAA (ie almost no risk) on the basis that they were diversified. AAA bonds are considered extremely safe, and can be invested in by the most conservative plans (ie pension plans). Of course, these CDOs weren't close to diversified -- they were all just bad mortgages -- but on paper they looked like they were made up of many different investments. The bottom tranches of these CDOs could be repackaged into more CDOs (called synthetic CDOs), to make them look more diversified/safe.

In the 90s, a lending company like Ameriprise would never think of giving a $700,000 mortgage with no money down to someone with a credit score of 450 and a $45,000 salary. It was too high-risk. However around 2003-2004 when the CDO market exploded, banks wanted as much raw material to make these MBSes as possible. They didn't care if it was a two-year deferred mortgage where the person had no intention or ability to pay when it came due, because banks were buying it no matter what. This, of course, drove up the price of the housing market.

The really stupid piece of all this was that the banks drank their own kool-aid. One department of a big bank would be repackaging the high-risk loans into low-risk CDOs. Another department of the same bank would be investing in CDOs made up of high-risk mortgages believing them to be low-risk.

tl;dr: Selling debt is normal. Selling high-risk debt as low-risk is not normal. Repackaging debt to sell it again and again is not normal.
